title: The Stuff You Should Know Doin’ Science Playlist: Things We Believed Before the Scientific Method
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck open the episode after a holiday break and introduce the 'Doin' Science' playlist episode on the scientific method, Episode seven of the series. They define science using William Harris's definition, distinguish quantitative and qualitative data, and compare inductive and deductive reasoning, using Edwin Hubble's discovery of galaxies beyond the Milky Way as an example. They explain the difference between colloquial and scientific meanings of 'theory' (with a Jerry bathroom-break example), then trace the history from the Dark Ages and the Renaissance through Aristotle, Roger Bacon, Francis Bacon, Leeuwenhoek and Hooke's microscopes, cell theory, and Virchow. Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment disproves spontaneous generation. The hosts walk through the steps of the scientific method (observation, question, hypothesis, controlled experiment with independent and dependent variables and control group, analysis, sharing results), discuss replication problems and publication bias, falsifiability and Karl Popper, the limits of science regarding the supernatural, and the line between science and value judgments. The episode closes with a listener mail about hybrid homeschooling and a sign-off.

segments.title: Holiday return and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck greet listeners after a December break, joke about a male enhancement pill ad and a stick of butter, and preview the episode on the scientific method and the Enlightenment tug of war between rationalism and mysticism.

segments.title: Defining science and data
segments.summary: The hosts use William Harris's definition of science as an intellectual and practical activity studying the physical and natural world through observation and experimentation. They note science is hands-on and that everyone uses scientific thinking. They discuss quantitative versus qualitative data and agree both are useful.

segments.title: Inductive and deductive reasoning
segments.summary: Chuck explains deductive reasoning as moving from a broad generalization to a specific case and inductive reasoning as moving from specific observations to a broad generalization, noting disagreement over inductive reasoning's role in science.

segments.title: Edwin Hubble and the expanding universe
segments.summary: Using Edwin Hubble at Mount Wilson's Hooker telescope as an example, the hosts describe how he observed nebulae that appeared to lie beyond the Milky Way and moving away, leading to the inductive idea of many expanding galaxies. Later testing supported it and it fed into the Big Bang theory.

segments.title: Science as a collective enterprise
segments.summary: Chuck explains that scientists rely on one another, citing journals and conferences, and that Hubble's observations were tested later by other scientists, turning his hypothesis into a theory.

segments.title: Hypothesis vs theory vs law
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the colloquial versus scientific meaning of 'theory'. Using a playful example about Jerry's bathroom breaks and Words with Friends, Chuck explains how a hypothesis becomes a theory after repeated support and a law after even wider support. They also reference the Explorables website.

segments.title: Dark Ages, Renaissance and rediscovery of Greek thought
segments.summary: The hosts describe the scientific slowdown of the Dark Ages, the role of the Islamic world and the Catholic Church, and the Renaissance's rediscovery of Aristotle, Euclid and Ptolemy. They discuss how Roger Bacon argued that Aristotle's writings were not automatically fact, and how Albertus Magnus favored experimentation over revealed truth.

segments.title: Francis Bacon and the Baconian method
segments.summary: Francis Bacon, a philosopher and attorney, is credited with laying out a systematic framework for investigation that became the basis of the scientific method, making science universal and repeatable. The hosts also mention the Shakespeare authorship theory tied to him.

segments.title: Microscopes, Hooke, Leeuwenhoek and cell theory
segments.summary: Lens grinding by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek led to microscopes. Robert Hooke used one to observe cork and describe cells, and Leeuwenhoek observed small animals. Schleiden concluded plants are made of cells, and Schwann extended this to animals, leading to the idea that all living things are made of cells.

segments.title: Virchow and spontaneous generation
segments.summary: Rudolf Virchow stated that cells come from pre-existing cells, challenging spontaneous generation. The hosts describe historical beliefs such as maggots spawning from rotten meat and mice from wheat in a sweaty shirt.

segments.title: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment
segments.summary: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in straight-neck and S-shaped-neck flasks. The straight-neck flask became cloudy while the S-neck stayed clear, which supported germs and disproved spontaneous generation. The hosts stress that this supported but did not prove cell theory, and that science disproves and supports rather than proves.

segments.title: Transition to the steps of the method
segments.summary: Josh introduces the steps of the scientific method after a brief message break, noting it is fluid and not on a laminated card.

segments.title: Observation, questions, and hypothesis
segments.summary: The hosts outline the first steps: observing, asking questions, and forming hypotheses. Darwin's study of Galapagos finches is the example of narrowing a question, and a car aerodynamics example illustrates a hypothesis written as an if-then statement that must be testable and falsifiable.

segments.title: Controlled experiments, variables, and analysis
segments.summary: The hosts explain independent and dependent variables, control groups, and keeping everything else identical, using the car shape wind tunnel example and Pasteur's flasks. They describe analyzing data and comparing results to the control.

segments.title: Sharing data and the replication problem
segments.summary: The hosts argue that sharing results is a missing step in most lists of the method. They cite an Economist article saying about half of published research cannot be replicated and a biotech firm reproduced only six of 53 cancer studies. They discuss confirmation bias, publication bias toward positive results, careerism, and peer review failures.

segments.title: Limits of the scientific method
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Karl Popper's falsifiability and how it separates science from pseudoscience. They argue that science cannot prove or disprove the supernatural, such as ghosts or God, and that science should not make value judgments, like telling people which car or light bulb to use.

segments.title: Listener review request
segments.summary: Josh asks listeners to leave a rating and review on iTunes and to tell one person about the show.

segments.title: Listener mail: hybrid homeschooling
segments.summary: Josh reads a text from his sister-in-law Jenny about hybrid homeschooling, in which students attend school two to three days a week, and mentions his niece Abby's volleyball and school activities. The hosts chat about the niece and volleyball.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Chuck gives contact information for social media, email and the website, and signs off with a reminder to visit HowStuffWorks.com.
